etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English comparatif, from Middle French comparatif, from Latin comparātīvus, equivalent to comparātus, from comparāre (“to compare”) + -ive, from Latin -īvus.

quote.citation: 1773, James Burnett, Of the Origin and Progress of Language:
quote.text: that kind of animals that have the comparative faculty, by which they compare things together, deliberate and resolve

definitions.definition: Using comparison as a method of study, or founded on something using it.

quote.citation: 1960 December, “Talking of Trains: The riding of B.R. coaches”, in Trains Illustrated, pages 705–706:
quote.text: After all, it is undeniable that the B.R. standard coach scored highly in comparative trials with other European railway vehicles on the Continent a few years ago, so that B.R. civil engineers must share responsibility for any defects in its behaviour over here.

quote.citation: 2016 October 24, Owen Gibson, “Is the unthinkable happening – are people finally switching the football off?”, in The Guardian‎[1], London:
quote.text: The Olympics, the weather and a comparative lack of heavyweight clashes so far this season have been cited as reasons for the drop in viewers.

quote.citation: 1837, William Whewell, History of the Inductive Sciences:
quote.text: The recurrence of comparative warmth and cold.

quote.citation: 1692, Richard Bentley, A Confutation of Atheism:
quote.text: This bubble,  […]  by reason of its comparative levity to the fluid that encloses it, would necessarily ascend to the top.
And need he had of slumber yet, for none / Had suffered more—his hardships were comparative / To those related in my grand-dad's Narrative.

definitions.definition: (grammar) A construction showing a relative quality, in English usually formed by adding more or appending -er. For example, the comparative of green is greener; of evil, more evil.
(grammar) A word in the comparative form.
(chiefly in the plural) Data used to make a comparison.

quote.citation: 2010, Barry Smith, Introductory Financial Accounting and Reporting, page 171:
quote.text: Investment ratios are positive. Comparative or trend data are required to draw final conclusions. The absence of comparatives and trend data constrains the conclusions.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An equal; a rival; a compeer.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1613, Nathan Field, John Fletcher, “Four Playes, or Morall Representations, in One”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act , (please specify the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Gerrard ever was / His full comparative.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) One who makes comparisons; one who affects wit.
